fields.description_1:
Gldrive needs to help learner drivers choose lessons before they have much experience with driving-school terms. Packages, prices, exam preparation and instructor information all influence the decision, but they should not arrive with equal weight. A new learner first needs to understand the available route and only then compare the practical details that belong to it.

The website therefore had to create a sequence from lesson choice to package information and booking or contact. Mobile users should be able to compare options without losing the main action below long explanations. The portfolio story also needed to avoid promises about pass rates, lesson counts or learning speed. The challenge was to make a driving-school offer feel straightforward while keeping the learning process honest and individual.
fields.description_2:
I organised Gldrive around the decisions a learner makes before booking: choose the lesson route, compare the relevant package information and then review exam or instructor details where they help. Pricing stays connected to the option it belongs to, so visitors do not have to reconstruct the offer from separate pages.

Booking and contact actions appear after enough context for someone to understand what they are asking about. I kept labels plain and the mobile order compact around cards, prices and next steps. The case description avoids claiming that a package guarantees a certain number of lessons or an exam result. It now explains how WordPress supports a clear driving-school journey without turning education outcomes into marketing promises.

fields.description_1:
Yco-it brings together IT support, security and compliance topics for business decision makers who may not know which discipline owns their problem. A company could arrive with a technical issue, a security concern or a compliance requirement, and technology language would make those routes harder to distinguish. The site needed to explain where each type of support fits before asking for contact.

Technical trust also had to be shown carefully. Security and compliance services cannot be described as guarantees, and specialist terms should not replace clear explanations. On mobile, service choices and evidence needed a hierarchy that stays readable. The portfolio problem was to make a multi-discipline IT offer understandable to non-specialists while keeping technical claims factual, scoped and connected to a practical next step.
fields.description_2:
I structured Yco-it around separate business questions for IT, security and compliance rather than one broad technology message. Each service route explains the type of need it addresses, with supporting technical or trust information placed after the first choice. This gives decision makers context before they reach an enquiry action.

I used direct labels and avoided absolute wording about security, compliance or business continuity because those outcomes depend on the environment and work performed. On smaller screens, service cards, proof and contact actions keep the same priority. Secondary information stays outside the main decision path. The portfolio case now shows how WordPress can organise a complex technical offer for business buyers without relying on generic expertise claims or promises that cannot be verified.

fields.description_1:
Bedrijfspostadres serves entrepreneurs who need a business address but may be comparing combinations of registration, post handling and scanning. The service seems simple until package details, account access and practical conditions are added. If presented without order, visitors may struggle to understand what is included before they sign up.

The website therefore needed to separate the core address service from package differences and explain what happens to incoming post. Signup should follow that comparison, not replace it. On mobile, package cards and practical information had to remain easy to scan. The portfolio story also needed to avoid claims about legal suitability or acceptance in every situation. The challenge was to make a practical business-address service understandable without hiding important conditions behind a quick signup route.
fields.description_2:
I organised Bedrijfspostadres around the steps an entrepreneur takes before choosing a package. The core address service is explained first, followed by post handling, scanning and the differences that matter between available options. Account and signup routes then appear where the visitor has enough context to choose deliberately.

I kept practical conditions close to the relevant package and avoided wording that suggests every address use case is automatically suitable or accepted. On smaller screens, package information, supporting details and actions follow a consistent order instead of becoming a wide comparison table. The portfolio case now explains the real WordPress service flow: understand the address offer, compare handling options and continue to signup, without generic claims about convenience or business outcomes.

fields.description_1:
Dmelektro works for homeowners and businesses that may arrive with an electrical problem, an installation project or a maintenance need. Those situations require different information, and a broad list of electrical services would not help visitors judge urgency, scope or the right next step. The site needed to separate planned work from support questions without asking users to diagnose faults.

Project and service information also had to stay factual because safety, timing and technical suitability depend on the installation. On mobile, people should be able to find the relevant service and contact route quickly. The portfolio challenge was to present electrical work in plain language, keep technical boundaries visible and guide visitors toward a useful enquiry without making promises about repairs or outcomes before inspection.
fields.description_2:
I structured Dmelektro around the type of electrical need rather than a single generic service page. Installation work, maintenance and other technical support have clear routes, with practical information introduced where it helps someone understand what to describe in an enquiry. This keeps the first choice simple while preserving technical context.

Contact actions remain visible after the relevant explanation, and I avoided wording that guarantees a diagnosis, repair time or result before the installation is assessed. On smaller screens, service sections and next steps keep a direct reading order. The portfolio case now reflects the real decision a customer makes when seeking electrical support: identify the type of need, review the relevant context and start a conversation with enough information for the next step.

fields.description_1:
Fixfinder has to help people describe a service need before they know which provider is suitable. The platform sits between a problem and a company, so it cannot assume that visitors understand service categories or what a provider needs. A directory would leave too much work to the user and make comparisons weaker.

The website therefore needed to guide people from the task itself to relevant provider information and a structured request. It also had to avoid suggesting that every provider has the same availability, price or quality. On mobile, the request path should stay short enough to complete without losing important context. The portfolio problem was to turn an uncertain service need into a clearer matching journey without promising a particular provider or outcome.
fields.description_2:
I organised Fixfinder around the problem a visitor wants solved. The first step is identifying the service need, after which the platform can show relevant provider context and collect the details required for a useful request. This makes matching the result of better information rather than simply displaying a list of companies.

Provider claims stay measured, and the structure does not imply identical pricing, availability or performance across businesses. On smaller screens, service choices, request fields and next steps follow a compact sequence so the flow remains manageable. I kept supporting information close to the point where it affects the match. The portfolio case now explains Fixfinder as a structured discovery and request platform, without generic marketplace language or unverified promises about outcomes.
